summary: CORE-Bench is a code-retrieval benchmark with three levels: L1 reuses existing snippet-level code-search sets, L2 maps SWE-bench-family issue/PR text to the pre-PR code chunks the patch edits (5,061 queries, 632 repos, 11 languages), and L3 adds broader-context labels mined from mini-SWE-agent browse traces and filtered by an LLM vote ensemble (2,580 queries, 106K labels). Embedding models that score high on L1 drop sharply on L2/L3; contrastive fine-tuning of Qwen3-Embedding on PRs from 628 non-SWE-bench repos raises L2/L3 substantially.

claims.claim: Embedding retrievers drop sharply from traditional code search to agentic-coding retrieval
claims.evidence: Table 3: Qwen3-Embedding-8B 71.7/96.9 (NDCG@10/R@100) on L1 vs 20.3/48.0 on L2 and 34.4/41.5 on L3; similar pattern across 11 listed models. Figure 4: L1 average only moderately correlates with L2.

claims.claim: Simple in-domain SFT significantly improves agentic-coding retrieval
claims.evidence: Table 3: Qwen3-8B-SFT L2 32.8/66.4 vs 20.3/48.0 base; L3 50.2/61.4 vs 34.4/41.5. Training repos stated disjoint from SWE-bench family (App. B). But SFT lowers L1 (8B: 71.7 -> 63.0 NDCG@10; 0.6B: 66.9 -> 58.1), a trade-off the text does not discuss; single training run, no variance.

claims.claim: Level-3 labels capture functionally useful context, not just textual relatedness
claims.evidence: Table 11: mini-SWE-agent resolve rate with reads restricted to L3 labels exceeds L2-only allowlist on all four sources (e.g. SWE-bench Verified 69.0% vs 62.0%; Multi-SWE-bench 39.5% vs 23.3%). Relative signal only; labels were produced by the same agent/model family that is then used to validate them, and relevance judged by an LLM vote (2x Qwen3.5-397B, 1x Claude Sonnet 4.6) with no human audit reported.
§3.1: L1 172K + L2 5,061 + L3 2,580 (approx. 179.6K by stated rounded figures); detail in Table 8. Count is dominated by recycled L1 snippet datasets, not the new agentic levels.

claims.claim: Java remains one of the harder L2 languages even after SFT
claims.evidence: Table 4/19 per-language NDCG@10 (e.g. Qwen3-0.6B Java L2 10.2 vs Python 18.4); stated in §4.5.

patterns.note: Off-the-shelf embedding retrieval is weak for issue-to-edit localization (L2 NDCG@10 ~3-22 for base models); domain SFT helps but stays far below L1.
BM25 L2 average 13.0/38.8 (Table 17) beats several dense models (bge-m3, gte-Qwen2, CodeRankEmbed) but trails Qwen3-Embedding-8B; grep/ls-style agent exploration itself is not benchmarked.
Built entirely from SWE-bench-family data; inherits its repo/language skew.

[retag 2026-10-08] Table 11 (App. F.2): mini-SWE-agent limited to Level-3 context mined from its own grep/cat exploration traces resolves more than when limited to Level-2 edit-site files (SWE-bench Verified 69.0% vs 62.0%, Multilingual 59.0 vs 43.0, Pro 43.2 vs 36.9, Multi-SWE-bench 39.5 vs 23.3). Unrestricted exploration scores higher still (73.0/65.0/46.1/42.0). So exploration finds useful context beyond the lines that get edited. But the labels come from the same agent's traces after an LLM vote (circular), with one agent and backbone, and embedding retrievers reach only ~34 NDCG@10 on that context (Table 3). No exploration agent is compared with a non-agent alternative.

methodology.sample: L1: ~172K queries from 8 existing datasets; L2: 5,061 queries over 632 repos and 9.38M chunks; L3: 2,580 queries, 106K qrels; SFT: 53,301 queries from 628 repos disjoint from SWE-bench
methodology.baselines: BM25 plus ~10 current general and code embedding models (Qwen3-Embedding, C2LLM-7B, SweRankEmbed-Large, jina-code, F2LLM-v2, e5-mistral, etc.); no rerankers, no hybrid, no agentic grep-based retrieval baseline
methodology.models: Embedding models only; Qwen3.5-397B-A17B used for filtering, rewriting, agent runs and 2 of 3 relevance votes; Claude Sonnet 4.6 as third vote
methodology.variance: None; single SFT run per size, no CIs
methodology.ablations: Query-rewrite variant, per-language, per-difficulty and per-intent breakdowns; no ablation of SFT negative sampling or epochs
methodology.contamination_controls: Temporal snapshot per query (corpus restricted to pre-PR state); SFT repos disjoint from SWE-bench family. No control for pretraining exposure of public SWE-bench repos in base embedding models.
methodology.languages: 11 languages in L2/L3 (Python, Go, JS, Rust, TS, Java, C++, C, Ruby, PHP, Swift); Python-heavy via SWE-bench sources

standards.artifacts: Abstract footnote states dataset on Hugging Face and evaluation code on GitHub (URLs not captured in extracted text); prompts in App. H

biases.detail: L3 relevance labels come from a 3-vote LLM ensemble (two votes from the same Qwen3.5 model) with no reported human agreement; validation in Table 11 is agent-based and relative.
Qwen3.5 builds/filters/rewrites the benchmark and the winning system is fine-tuned Qwen3-Embedding; Qwen-family authorship overlap (see coi).
No seeds or confidence intervals for SFT or evaluation.
Measures single-shot embedding retrieval, while the paper's own intro says agent harnesses actually retrieve via ls/grep/iterative narrowing; no end-to-end agent success with each retriever.
SWE-bench repositories are public and widely used; base embedding models may have seen them.
SFT reduces L1 performance by ~8-9 NDCG points; not discussed.

coi.affiliations: Beihang University (Institute of AI; SKLCCSE) and Peking University listed. Four authors (Yanzhao Zhang, Mingxin Li, Dingkun Long, Pengjun Xie) have no affiliation in the extracted text; the cited Qwen3-Embedding paper (arXiv 2506.05176) lists Y. Zhang, M. Li, D. Long, P. Xie among its authors.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Qwen3-Embedding (base and fine-tuned) is the top-performing family; Qwen3.5 used to build the benchmark
coi.detail: Likely overlap between benchmark authors and the developers of the best-performing embedding family, with that affiliation undisclosed in the paper. Mitigated by many third-party baselines and a peer-reviewed venue; headline conclusion (all embedders drop on L2/L3) does not favor any vendor.

verdict_reason: Solid, peer-reviewed benchmark with many baselines and per-language breakdowns; the main finding (snippet-search scores do not predict issue-to-edit retrieval) is well supported. Caveats: L3 labels are LLM-judged without human audit, no variance, retrieval measured in isolation from agents, undisclosed probable Qwen-team involvement, and the SFT L1 regression is unmentioned.
applicability: For a Java team choosing between embedding RAG and lexical/agentic search in its harness: do not trust general code-search leaderboards; generic embedders localize edits poorly (Java is among the hardest L2 languages, Table 4) and BM25 is competitive with several of them. If the team adds embedding retrieval over its >=4 ingestion repositories, expect gains only from fine-tuning on its own PR history (the L2-style recipe in App. B is reusable), and evaluate on its own issues-to-diffs. Cross-repo retrieval, spec documents, and healthcare content are not covered (each query is single-repo). The paper is host-neutral; nothing ties it to a specific agent host.
